title: Hard hearts in a boat (Mark 8:11–21)
hook: they've forgotten bread and worry, after two feedings

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven baskets: four thousand fed in Gentile country. Your line was enough again. Who outside your circle did you feed? Day one hundred ninety-one.

You get to the checkout and realize you left your wallet at home. Or you're halfway to the airport and wonder if you packed the passport. That little drop in your stomach. That's the disciples today. They're in the boat, crossing the lake again, and somebody looks in the bag. They forgot the bread. There's only one loaf. And while they're quietly panicking about lunch, Jesus is trying to tell them something important. They completely miss it. Mark tells this scene with a kind of frustrated love. Today: hard hearts in a boat.
screen: `WALLET LEFT AT HOME.` → `ONLY ONE LOAF IN THE BOAT.` → `THEY MISS WHAT HE SAYS.`

segments.voice: Just before they sailed, some Pharisees had asked Jesus for a sign from heaven, proof on demand. He sighed deeply and refused: no sign will be given to this generation. Now in the boat he warns, in the old King James Bible: "Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod." Leaven, you might remember from day twenty-four, is the bit of old dough that works invisibly through a whole batch. He means an attitude that spreads: demanding proof, playing power games. And the disciples say to each other, he's talking about bread because we forgot to bring any. So he asks them a string of questions, and they come fast: "perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?" Then a quiz. When I broke five loaves for five thousand, how many baskets of leftovers? Twelve, they say. And the seven for four thousand? Seven. And he says, "How is it that ye do not understand?" That's where Mark leaves it. No answer. They've watched thousands fed, twice, and they're worried about lunch with him sitting right there. And notice the one loaf in the boat. Many readers hear a quiet hint: they're not as short of bread as they think, because the one who feeds crowds is on board. Christians find this scene uncomfortably familiar. We forget what we've already been carried through, and the next worry feels like the first.
screen: `NO SIGN FOR THIS GENERATION.` · `BEWARE THE LEAVEN.` · `TWELVE BASKETS, THEN SEVEN.` · `ONE LOAF, AND HE'S ON BOARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember one time you had enough. Settle, and breathe. Go back to a time you were sure you wouldn't make it. Money was short, or time, or strength, or hope. And somehow there was enough. Someone showed up. A door opened. You got through. Stay with that memory. Count the baskets, so to speak: what was left over afterward? Now hold it next to whatever you're worried about today. If you pray, you can give thanks for that time. The bell holds the time.
Hard hearts in a boat. The disciples, after two feedings, panicking over one loaf, and Jesus asking them to remember.

segments.voice: Your line: do you not yet understand? Today, when a worry comes, remember one time there was enough, before you panic. Day one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Many Christians keep a habit of remembering God's help in the past, through gratitude journals, testimonies or prayers of thanksgiving, as a way of meeting present worries.

fork.reveal: the disciples think it's about bread. he meant a spreading attitude, and asks: do ye not remember? the baskets?

original.note: Greek: leaven, old dough kept back to raise a new batch, a small thing that spreads.

trapdoor: what you thought: the disciples just forgot their lunch.
what it means: after two feedings they still panic over bread, with the one who fed thousands sitting in the boat.
what a scholar hears: Mark 8:17–18 echoes the prophets on eyes that don't see and ears that don't hear, and Mark leaves the question open.
